speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: These laws are currently contained within the Betting and Sweepstake Duties Act, or BSDA, and the Private Lotteries Act, or PLA.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Since then, we have made improvements in our tax administration and enforcement.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: For tax administration, the Commissioner of Betting Duties, currently, does not have the power to refund overpaid betting and sweepstake duties, even though that is provided for overpaid private lotteries duty and other taxes administered by IRAS.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Clause 19 of the Bill will now provide for the Commissioner of Gambling Duties to do so.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: For enforcement of the betting and sweepstake duties, the Commissioner of Betting Duties, currently, may not enter or search premises.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: However, he may do so for private lotteries duty and all other taxes administered by IRAS.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, clause 25 of the Bill provides for the Commissioner of Gambling Duties to similarly enter and search premises for the enforcement of betting and sweepstake duties.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The Bill also harmonises, for gambling duties, what constitutes an offence; and raises the fines and penalties for the gambling duties which have remained unchanged since the 1950s.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Today, for betting and sweepstake duties, it is not a specific offence for a taxpayer to file an incorrect statement.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: If any prosecution is to take place for false filing of returns for betting and sweepstake duties, we rely on general criminal law, as in the Penal Code, which has a penalty designed to apply generally.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: On the other hand, the filing of incorrect returns for private lotteries duty and casino tax has each been made a specific offence.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Likewise, for the filing of incorrect returns in connection with other taxes, like income tax or GST.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, this Bill proposes that the filing of an incorrect statement for betting and sweepstake duties will be a specific offence with a penalty that is consistent with similar specific offences in the other tax laws.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: For example, the fines in BSDA and PLA are, currently, not aligned for the same offences.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: For failing to file a return, a betting operator could face a fine of up to $500 and a private lottery promoter could face a fine of $1,000.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Clauses 27, 28, 29 and 30 of the Bill ensure similar penalty structures across gambling taxes and that the quanta of penalties and fines are commensurate with similar offences in other tax Acts administered by IRAS.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: As a related amendment, clause 46 of the Bill makes amendments to the Casino Control Act.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: I will explain the amendments for the casino tax, and Minister of State Alvin Tan will speak later on the revisions to the exclusivity period and divestment restrictions.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Currently, gross gaming revenue is subject to casino tax rates of 5% for premium gaming and 15% for mass gaming.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: These rates are not to be changed until after 28 February 2022.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In April 2019, the Government announced the introduction of a tiered casino tax structure from 1 March 2022 with higher tax rates than today and a new 10-year moratorium, subject to the casino operator meeting certain development targets.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: For mass gaming, the first $3.1 billion of gross gaming revenue per year will be taxed at 18% and the rest at 22%.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: If the casino operator fails to satisfactorily meet its development targets, a flat rate of 12% for premium gaming and 22% for mass gaming will apply instead.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, clause 46 of the Bill provides for these amendments.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: These amendments are found in clause 48 of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Would the Minister share what has been the average annual gross revenues from local and foreign visitors respectively in premium gaming and mass gaming during the pre-COVID-19 pandemic and in the past two years?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: What has been the average gaming revenue per local visitor and for each foreign visitor in both premium and mass gaming pre-COVID-19 and in the past two years?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: What about the expected completion of the two integrated resorts' extension and projected increase in revenue with the expansion and the increase in economic contribution, including all related supporting industries?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: My speech today will focus largely on the related amendments to the Casino Control Act, which I believe to be the most significant change within this Bill.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: But I will, first, speak broadly about the issue of problem gambling as well as gambling duties in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Speak of gambling and some of the images that appear in my mind are the advertisements run by the National Council on problem gambling featuring the 2012 TV commercial where a man was asking his daughter for her piggy bank and saying, "One more try and I will give it all back".

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Or the other advertisement featuring Andy, whose father bet all his savings on Germany.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: All these advertisements were the subject of numerous light-hearted parodies and spoofs, especially after Germany won the World Cup in 2014.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The issue of problem gambling and the social ills associated with it are a serious one that deserves our utmost priority whenever the topic of gambling is discussed.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: As a result of COVID-19, however, I wonder if and how much did visitorship increase as a result of border restrictions.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Further, to those at higher risk of problem gambling, the higher entry levy could instead spur them to raise their bets to cover the additional cost of entry.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: So, I do hope that the Government will continue to tighten the safeguards not just against casino visitorship for locals, but to other forms of gambling as well, particularly online gambling.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I have been receiving weekly SMSes and WhatsApp messages inviting me to online casinos, for example, and I am sure a number of Members would have as well.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: And just last month, the news about three brothers operating an illegal gambling syndicate that collected a weekly revenue of at least $1 million suggests that urgent action needs to be taken to address the shadow gambling scene in Singapore as well.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Moving on to the legalised aspects of things, gambling or betting taxes, alongside tobacco and liquor excise duties, play a not insignificant role in the Government's operating revenues over the years.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Even with the onset of COVID-19, with suspension of betting activity during the circuit breaker period and the sharp fall in tourist arrivals affecting visitorship, the estimated FY2020 betting tax revenue was at $1.8 billion.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This is larger than the contribution from tobacco excise duties of $1.2 billion in FY2019 and $1.4 billion in FY2020.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Yet, at the same time, revenues from betting taxes have been relatively range-bound over the past decade, with contributions from betting taxes not too different in FY2010 at about $2.3 billion.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In fact, I observe that the relative share of betting taxes to the Government's operating revenues has broadly been declining over the last 20 years, from close to 6% of revenues in FY2002 to 3% of revenues in FY2021.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Given the social objective of avoiding excessive consumption of areas, such as betting, tobacco and liquor, I strongly believe that there is room for betting taxes to be raised.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I recognise, of course, that part of the consequential amendments to this Bill is the raising of casino taxes, a point which I will revisit shortly in my speech.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I note that the last time betting duty rates on lotteries were raised was more than seven years ago in July 2014, from 25% to 30% of gross bets.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Would the Government consider raising betting duty rates and other associated gambling duty rates in the near-term in this regard?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I will next touch on amendments to the Casino Control Act, the most notable of which, in my view, is the raising of casino tax rates, which are slated to take effect from 1 March 2022.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I am supportive of the raising of casino tax rates and my first question is: what are the Government's expectations of the additional revenues from higher casino taxes, not just in the next financial year, but over the next decade?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I ask this because, back when the two IRs were awarded, the Government had committed not to raise the casino tax for at least 15 years.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: As we are coming to the end of the moratorium in February 2022, the Government will also be providing a moratorium on the new casino tax rates, this time, for a 10-year period.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The recency of COVID-19 and the significant curtailment of visitor arrivals into Singapore could lead some quarters to question the sustainability of the higher casino tax rates, in the sense of whether or not the tax rate increase could place an onerous burden on the two casino operators, amidst ongoing uncertainties, given the effects of COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: But if we take a step back, I would argue that higher casino tax rates are not only long overdue but could have room to grow in future.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I am reminded of the buzz that surrounded the opening of the two IRs back in 2010, which have, no doubt, enhanced Singapore's position as a tourist destination and the two operators have also done well for themselves, surprising many back in those days, given how both IRs have achieved success very early on in their operations.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: According to an article in My Paper in June 2010, the late Minister Mentor Lee Kuan Yew shared that Marina Bay Sands will probably take three to seven years to reach a capacity that can help spur Singapore's tourism and convention industries.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The late Mr Sheldon Adelson, former Chairman of Las Vegas Sands, however, said that Minister Mentor Lee was being a little too pessimistic and the property would be up and running at full speed the next year.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Mr Adelson was proven right in the end and, I believe, even surpassed his own expectations.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: He shared in a statement in 2011 that Marina Bay Sands (MBS) had generated over US$1 billion of adjusted property EBITDA in just its first 12 months of operation, which is a record not only for any property in the history of Sands, but a record for any property in the history of the industry.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Both properties continue to generate strong earnings and cash flow today, which will, in all likelihood, recover alongside Singapore's tourism industry.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Macau, the largest gaming market globally, imposes a special gaming tax of 35% of GGR, amidst other fixed and variable premiums payable, while also requiring operators to contribute a further percentage of GGR to utilities designated by the Macau government.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In this context, could there have been room for our casino tax rates to be higher?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This, considering also the strong profitability of both IRs, where the recent impact from COVID-19 notwithstanding, both IRs have, historically, generated 40% to 50% EBITDA margins since their opening.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The third point I would like to raise in relation to the Casino Control Act is related to a Parliamentary Question (PQ) I filed in November where I had asked the Minister for Trade and Industry, given COVID-19 disruptions to the hospitality industry, whether there are any changes to the timeline investment commitment and nature of the S$9 billion combined investment commitment by the two IRs.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: While COVID-19 has, indeed, created significant disruptions and delays for the construction industry, how much leeway is the Government prepared to give the two IRs?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Are there any revisions to the Government's required completion dates and what sort of timeline would be deemed reasonable?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I am sure, for Singaporeans looking forward to the new attractions and the IRs themselves alike, regulatory clarity and certainty on key deadlines would be much appreciated, not least because a flat tax rate will be applied if the IRs fail to meet their investment commitments.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Last but not least, with casino taxes set to rise, how much of the increased revenues from our raised casino taxes would be diverted towards efforts to mitigate the negative social effects of the continued existence of gambling establishments in this country?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I would also humbly suggest that perhaps a fixed percentage or absolute amount of gambling revenues could be dedicated towards gambling safeguards and rehabilitation of problem gamblers.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I also note that in the 2019 press statement, it was revealed that the IRs will conduct a joint study with MSF to understand upstream preventive technologies and options available to promote responsible gaming among all gamblers.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: What has been the findings of this study, what measures will be introduced following the study and will the report be shared with the public?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: All in all, I do support the rise in casino tax rates, though I believe there is still upside room to go when it comes to raising taxes, especially given the social objective of avoiding its excessive consumption.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: And I hope the Government will consider the points raised in my speech.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I have three points of clarifications to raise.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My first point is on the remission of gambling duties.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister clarify under what circumstances will gambling duties be considered incompatible with the purposes of the Act?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Further, the Minister may delegate the exercise of his or her powers in relation to remission to a Commissioner or public officer.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister clarify if there are limits to the categories of public officers to whom the Minister's powers can be delegated?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My second point is on the amount of penalty tax that can be imposed on outstanding gambling duties.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I agree that the amount of penalty tax should not be excessive for an individual.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: That said, can the Minister share what enforcement tools are available to the Ministry for the recovery of gambling duties if these remained unpaid even after the maximum amount of penalty tax has been reached?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister also share what softer measures are available for the Ministry to work with an indebted individual to meet his or her debts?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My final point is the effect of the present Bill on Singapore's public policy on gambling.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: While the cases concerned the enforcement of gambling debts which were incurred abroad, a relevant issue considered in these cases is the local policy position on gambling.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In those cases, the Court had also considered local legislation on gambling, including the Gaming Act, Casino Control Act and Common Gaming Houses Act.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister clarify if the consolidation of laws on levies and collection of duties on lawful betting and lotteries have any effect on the public policy position on gambling in Singapore?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: If so, how should the Government's position on gambling be understood?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In summary, I hope the Minister can shed light on my clarifications relating to the remission of gambling duties, the imposition of penalty taxes and Singapore's public policy on gambling.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: With the unprecedented roll-out of various assistance schemes, free vaccination drives and increased healthcare burden amidst the COVID-19 pandemic, many Singaporeans have come to acknowledge the importance of having adequate Government revenue and savings in our reserves.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: There is also greater scrutiny of the Government's fiscal policies on how monies are spent and on the sources of income.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It helps to minimise discrepancies and misappropriation of funds.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I appreciate the details on short levying, erroneous funding and overpayment in the various sections, as well as the recovering and refunding of shortfalls.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: First, Mr Deputy Speaker, Sir, will the active detection and enforcement of actions against underpayments and other discrepancies require significantly more manpower and resources?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How will the Ministry ensure that IRAS is able to cope with the additional responsibilities?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How does IRAS fulfil the complex requirements of bookkeeping and following up with discrepancies?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Are there plans to deploy smart technology to support their operations?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: If so, are there safeguards to ensure that such information will only be used for the purposes of collection of gambling duties and that the data is not compromised?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Second, Mr Deputy Speaker, Sir, how will this Bill affect Singapore Sweep retailers and vendors?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: My main concern is for the small-time vendors and franchisees who sell Big Sweep and lottery tickets in the heartlands.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Would the amendments to the tax administration scheme require any action on their part?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Can the Ministry clarify whether this tax is already incorporated into the costs that they incurred from obtaining the selling rights and tickets from Singapore Pools?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How will this affect them, especially with regard to their earnings?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Lastly, we need to be mindful of the costs involved as a result of the Bill changes.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: A concern is that costs may be wasted on applications for assessment, reassessment of liability and appeals, based on similar facts from earlier cases.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Furthermore, decisions and appeals made publicly available may allow appellants to discern whether to appeal, if the said appellants are made aware of previous decisions and facts hitherto.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: As such, will information of the appeals and decisions by the Commissioner or the Minister be published and made publicly available?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The Bill is silent as to the costs against assessment, reassessment of liability and appeal.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: In this connection, would cost consequence against the taxable person be necessary to prevent frivolous applications?

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: When the IRs were first introduced, we provided an exclusivity period of 10 years, during which the Government would not introduce any other casinos.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: This was necessary as the IRs had made substantial investments and needed some business certainty.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Marina Bay Sands (MBS) will introduce a state-of-the-art entertainment arena which would host world-class performances and an iconic new tower comprising hotel and rooftop attractions.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: There will also be additional MICE space to host exhibitions and conventions.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Resorts World Sentosa (RWS) will expand Universal Studios Singapore by almost 20% with two new themed zones – Minion Park and Super Nintendo World – and create a new Singapore Oceanarium.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: It will also redevelop its waterfront promenade and introduce a driverless transport system along the Sentosa Boardwalk to improve accessibility into Sentosa.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: These investments will enhance the attractiveness and tourism appeal of Singapore, amid stronger competition for travellers post-pandemic.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Singaporeans can also look forward to more lifestyle and entertainment options.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: As an example, last week, I witnessed the launch of the Resorts World Sentosa and the National University of Singapore (NUS) Living Laboratory project.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: The living lab brings together NUS' capabilities as a leading global research institute and RWS' strengths as a world-class tourism destination.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: The project focuses on biodiversity and energy conservation and will help preserve and restore our natural heritage.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: This is in line with our Singapore Green Plan 2030 and Sentosa Development Corporation's plans to transform Sentosa into a carbon-neutral destination by 2030.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Again, it will, in turn, enhance Sentosa's appeal as a tourism and conservation destination.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: These are hefty investments and a further extension of the exclusivity period was required, as the casino is a small but essential part of the IR in that it makes the larger development and slew of activities which I mentioned earlier financially viable.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: The duration of the exclusivity period was arrived at after considering factors, such as what the parties could offer, the social impact, competitive dynamics and what the IRs deemed necessary from a financial viability viewpoint.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Clause 46(1) amends section 41 of the Casino Control Act to introduce this exclusivity period.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Clause 46(2) amends section 42 of the Casino Control Act to reflect this updated exclusivity period.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: This is because non-gaming areas will expand by a much larger amount.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: As a pre-emptive measure to minimise the social impact of problem gambling, the Government raised the casino entry levies for Singaporeans and Permanent Residents by 50% in April 2019.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: In response to Mr Gan Thiam Poh and Mr Louis Chua's questions on the expected completion of the two IR expansions, the IRs remain committed to the expansion plans.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: However, with the disruption that COVID-19 has had on the construction industry, both IRs have indicated that there will be potential delays in the completion of their projects.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: And this is not altogether surprising or unique to this project or this industry.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: COVID-19 has impacted construction timelines, both locally and globally.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: As the COVID-19 situation continues to evolve and, in fact, is evolving, and the IRs' expansions are complex multi-year projects, the full extent of the delay is not yet clear.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: This will enhance Singapore's tourism appeal, provide more entertainment options and jobs for Singaporeans and benefit local businesses.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: To this end, clauses 46(1) and 46(2) of the Gambling Duties Bill make amendments to the Casino Control Act related to the exclusivity period.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Mr Yip Hon Weng asked whether the Bill will create significant additional resourcing needs for IRAS.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: First, the Bill consolidates and streamlines laws that are, currently, contained within the BSDA and PLA.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, many of these functions are already performed by IRAS today.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Second, where there are new functions like electronic serving of notices, or the ability to enter and search premises for the enforcement of betting and sweepstake duties, these functions are not new to IRAS.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: IRAS, currently, performs these functions for the other taxes that it administers and has the requisite capabilities.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Mr Yip Hong Weng also asked if IRAS has plans to use smart technology to support its operations.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: IRAS already does this and will continue to do so.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The consequential amendment to the IRAS Act in this Bill to provide for an electronic service system paves the way for e-services for betting and casino operators and private lottery promoters.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: More generally, IRAS is developing new artificial intelligence applications to enhance and automate key processes for the taxes that it administers.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: IRAS will continue to improve on its administration and enforcement to keep it efficient and effective.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Mr Louis Ng asked what enforcement tools are available to IRAS for the recovery of unpaid gambling duties and where the maximum penalties have already been reached.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: He also asked what softer measures are available for an indebted individual to meet his tax obligations.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The taxpayers for the three types of betting taxes – casino tax, private lotteries duty and betting and sweepstake duties – are business providers of gaming and, generally, not individuals acting in their individual capacity.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: If the need arises to recover unpaid betting taxes, the tools available for IRAS include suing the taxpayer or appointing someone who holds money for the taxpayer, such as a bank, to pay the sum to the Commissioner.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: If an individual is indebted, IRAS will explore a payment arrangement with the indebted individual to meet his or her debts.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: As to Mr Yip Hon Weng's suggestion to require an appellant to pay costs to prevent frivolous applications for assessment, reassessment of liability and appeals, such frivolous applications are not an issue, currently, for betting taxes.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, we do not charge taxpayers who apply to IRAS for revising their tax assessments.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Mr Yip Hon Weng asked how we protect taxpayer data.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: A corresponding provision already exists in most other tax Acts.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: It is an offence to share confidential information except in certain specified circumstances.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Authorised persons who are granted access to taxpayer data are required to make and subscribe to a declaration of secrecy.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Even without a specific confidentiality provision, taxpayer income information is protected by the common law duty of confidentiality, the Official Secrets Act and the data protection regime under the Public Sector (Governance) Act.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Mr Louis Ng asked about the remission of gambling duties.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: This pertains to clause 12(1) of the Bill which provides for remission when the gambling duties are incompatible with the purposes of the Act.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: This Ministerial power to remit taxes is a provision that is present in other existing tax Acts like the GST Act, the Income Tax Act, the Property Tax Act and the Stamp Duties Act.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, it is a generic provision that we have in our tax Acts.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: While it is unlikely that such remission power will be invoked for gambling duties, we have, nevertheless, provided for this remission power for gambling duties in the remote event that such an unforeseen situation should arise.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Now, let me touch on the broader impact of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Mr Yip Hon Weng asked whether small-scale vendors and franchisees, especially those who sell Big Sweep and lottery tickets in the heartlands, will be affected.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: For the individual retailers, the amendments do not require any additional action on their part and, because there is no change in the rates of duty, the amendments will also not impact their earnings.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: There is no change that we are proposing for now, but we will continue to review the betting tax regime, as we do for other taxes on a regular basis.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Our objective is to ensure that betting taxes are high enough to manage gambling demand and, at the same time, that operators and promoters can compete effectively against illegal gambling operators.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I turn now to Mr Yip Hon Weng and Mr Gan Thiam Poh's questions on the revenue collection associated with the changes in this Bill.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: On the casino tax, Mr Gan Thiam Poh asked about the gaming revenue from local and foreign visitors for premium and mass gaming.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We do not collect data on the proportion of casino tax from local and foreign visitors.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: This is because casino tax does not differentiate between whether the individual concerned is a local or a foreigner.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I am unable, unfortunately, to share the details of casino tax collections.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Casino tax revenue is included under a broader classification of betting taxes which also includes taxes from lotteries, horse and sports betting and fruit machines.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: As for Mr Gan Thiam Poh's question on the projected increase in revenue with the expansion and increase in economic contribution, I believe this has been covered by Minister of State Alvin Tan when he talked about the expected economic benefits of IRs in his speech.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We have, on multiple occasions, articulated our approach towards problem gambling and this position remains unchanged.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Mr Louis Chua also asked about resources to address this and I would like to assure him that the Government will ensure that sufficient resources are set aside to deal with problem gambling.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Number one is, with COVID-19, whether endemic or pandemic, there is a lot less travel, especially in business travel.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: So, I wanted to know, in terms of jobs created and the MICE industry and tourism management expertise that we were supposed to acquire as a result of the IR policy – how has this physical IR model actually benefited the Singapore economy.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The second is that we all know that there is a rapid rise of online gambling.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: And I wanted to ask the Minister how the gambling duties for this rapidly rising source of gambling revenue are collected and whether more attention is applied to the space of online gambling because, actually, over the last 10 to 15 years, a lot of things have changed, in fact.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: This is with regard to the overall tourism strategy and our strategy with regard to MICE.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: I would say that, as Members are aware, the tourism sector, be it the aviation sector or the associated sectors, have been hard hit by COVID-19 due to travel restrictions and safe management measures (SMMs).

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: But that does not mean that we should hold back or not invest in our tourism capabilities and capacity for the long run.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: This is because the tourism landscape, as I mentioned earlier, is getting competitive and we must position ourselves for when tourism upticks, for when regular travel resumes and for when events, such as MICE, tourism, start to resume some form of normalcy.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: And that is why the IRs are expanding.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: And most of the offerings are catered towards tourism and developing this capability for when tourism and travel resume.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And if technology continues to make it easier for people to gamble anywhere and everywhere, then such illegal online gambling may continue to grow.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I think Mr Louis Chua also highlighted this in his speech.
